kurals.tamil:
கூறாமை நோக்கக் குறிப்பறிவான் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
மாறாநீர் வையக் கணி.
kurals.transliteration:
Kooraamai nokkak kurippu-arivaan enjnjaandrum
Maaraaneer vaiyak kani.
kurals.meaning: The person who looks at someone and understands what they intend, without a word being said, is at all times an ornament to this sea-girt world.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your friend comes to school looking quiet and droopy. Nobody says anything, but you notice, sit next to them, and share your snack. You understood without being told. Valluvar says a person who can do that is like a jewel the whole world wears.
kurals.university: The chapter opens a sequence in the Amaicciyal (section on ministers) that follows directly on ‘Conduct in the Presence of the King’ (ch. 70): having learned how near to stand, the minister must now learn to read the ruler’s unspoken kurippu (intention, inner purpose shown by outward sign). Parimelazhagar reads the subject as the minister and the object as the king: kooraamai (without his saying it) and nokka (by looking, i.e., at the face and eyes) he knows the intent, and such a man is ani (ornament, jewel) to the vaiyam (earth) whose maaraaneer (never-failing water, the ocean) surrounds it; enjnjaandrum means ‘at all times’. The hyperbole of ‘ornament to the world’ rather than ‘to the court’ signals that this faculty is rare and universally prized. The same title, Kurippu Arithal, reappears as chapter 110 in the Kamattuppal, where lovers read each other’s glances; commentators note the deliberate echo between political and amorous sign-reading. The standard text reads nokka; one online sandhi edition prints நோக்ககிக், evidently a misprint for நோக்கக் (some editions give நோக்கிக், with the same sense).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He shall also endeavour to read the mind and appearance of the king.”
hinduism.explanation: In the chapter on how a courtier serves the ruler, Kautilya makes reading the king’s mood from his looks and movements a standing duty of the minister.
hinduism.tie_back: Kautilya names the same skill Valluvar praises: knowing the ruler’s intent from his appearance before he speaks.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Same setting (minister and king) and the same skill; Kautilya treats it as a duty, Valluvar as a crowning virtue.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore the king said unto me, Why is thy countenance sad, seeing thou art not sick? this is nothing else but sorrow of heart.”
christianity.explanation: King Artaxerxes sees his cupbearer Nehemiah’s face and correctly reads grief in his heart before Nehemiah has said anything.
christianity.tie_back: A royal court scene in which the unspoken heart is read from the face, as the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong parallel in act, though here the king reads the servant rather than the servant reading the king.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes needy people too dignified to beg; the careless think they are fine, but the perceptive recognise their need from outward signs.
islam.tie_back: The praised person is the one who knows a need that is never spoken, just as the Kural praises reading the unsaid.
islam._accuracy_note: Close in principle; the Qur’an applies it to charity rather than to statecraft.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Joseph came in unto them in the morning, and saw them, and, behold, they were sad. And he asked Pharaoh’s officers ... saying: ‘Wherefore look ye so sad to-day?’”
judaism.explanation: Joseph, a prisoner, notices from their faces that Pharaoh’s butler and baker are troubled, and that attentiveness leads to his interpreting their dreams and later to his rise at court.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph’s rise begins with reading unspoken trouble on a face, the very skill the Kural says makes a man a jewel.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good narrative match; Joseph still asks aloud, whereas the Kural’s ideal needs no question.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘Such is your thinking, here is where your thinking is, thus is your mind.’ And however much he may read, that’s exactly how it is, and not otherwise.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists reading another’s mind, first of all by means of a sign, as one of three recognised wonders, and says the accurate reader is never wrong.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism likewise treats accurately knowing another’s unspoken mind as a rare and admired power.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 3.60, Sangarava Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: The sutta’s mind-reading is partly supernormal and is ranked below teaching, whereas Valluvar describes a natural, trained perceptiveness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “No one noticed his distress except Alcinous, who was sitting near him, and heard the heavy sighs that he was heaving.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus hides his tears under his cloak while the bard sings of Troy; only King Alcinous perceives his grief and tactfully ends the song.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Alcinous is the Kural’s ornament in action: he understands a guest’s silent sorrow and acts on it without being asked.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close: unspoken feeling read by attention alone, and the reader is honoured for his tact.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius that a person’s character can be gathered from the smallest things: the way they walk, move a hand, answer, or carry their face.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, outward signs are constant evidence of the inner man for anyone who pays attention.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca supports the Kural’s premise that the attentive can know a mind without being told.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 52 (trans. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of Letter 52; about reading character rather than a ruler’s passing intention.

kurals.tamil:
ஐயப் படாஅது அகத்தது உணர்வானைத்
தெய்வத்தோ டொப்பக் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aiyap padaaadhu akaththadhu unarvaanaith
Theyvaththodu oppak kolal.
kurals.meaning: The one who perceives, without any doubt, what lies inside another’s mind should be regarded as equal to a god.
kurals.elementary: Some grown-ups seem to know exactly what you are feeling before you say it, and they are always right. It can feel almost magical. Valluvar says a person who can truly do that deserves to be honoured almost like a god.
kurals.university: Aiyap padaaadhu uses alapedai (metrical vowel lengthening, படாஅது for படாது) to stretch ‘without doubting’, stressing certainty rather than guesswork. Akaththadhu is ‘that which is within’ (akam = interior, mind), and unarvaan ‘one who perceives’. Parimelazhagar explains the comparison theyvaththodu oppa (as equal to a deity): to know the heart directly is a faculty proper to the divine, so a man who has it without error shares a divine attribute, though he remains human (Mu. Varadarasanar adds ‘even though he is a man’). Kalaignar makes the logic explicit: if such knowledge belongs to God, the man who has it may be likened to God. The couplet should be read with 701 as a rising scale: ornament to the world, then peer of the gods. No significant textual variants; the sandhi text reads படாஅ தகத்த துணர்வானைத்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that he knows all beings, past, present and to come, while no one truly knows him.
hinduism.explanation: Complete knowledge of every being’s inner life is presented as a mark of the divine.
hinduism.tie_back: If knowing hearts fully is God’s own trait, the Kural’s claim that such a person is like a god follows naturally.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Supports the premise (knowing minds is divine) but says nothing about human mind-readers.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
christianity.explanation: God tells Samuel that humans judge by looks, but God sees the heart directly.
christianity.tie_back: Seeing into the heart is God’s way of seeing, so a person who does it without doubt comes close to the divine, as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on heart-knowledge as divine, though the verse sets human sight against God’s rather than praising gifted people.

islam.quote_or_event: “He knows that which deceives the eyes and what the breasts conceal.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names knowledge of hidden glances and concealed thoughts as one of God’s attributes.
islam.tie_back: Knowing what the breast conceals is described as God’s knowledge, which is why the Kural compares its human possessor to a deity.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on the divine attribute; Islam would not call any human equal to God, so the comparison is only partial.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud reads Isaiah 11:3 as saying the Messiah will ‘smell and judge’, knowing the truth without evidence, and reports that Bar Koziba was rejected when he could not do this.
judaism.explanation: Knowing guilt or innocence without witnesses is treated as a sign of divinely endowed, messianic status.
judaism.tie_back: As in the Kural, knowing what is inside without doubt raises a person above the ordinary toward the divine.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in structure (certain inner knowledge equals quasi-divine status); the context is messianic, not ministerial.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Among the Tathagata’s powers the Buddha lists knowing, as it really is, the dispositions and faculties of other beings.
buddhism.explanation: Accurate knowledge of others’ inner tendencies is counted among the powers that mark a fully awakened one.
buddhism.tie_back: Buddhism, like the Kural, places flawless knowledge of other minds among the highest, near-superhuman attainments.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel in esteem; the Buddhist power is spiritual attainment, not courtly perception.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The Delphic oracle tells Croesus’ envoys that Apollo knows the number of the sands and the measure of the sea, understands the mute and hears those who do not speak.
greek_mythology.explanation: The god’s power shows in knowing what is unspoken; Croesus’ test of the oracles turns on it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In Greek myth, hearing the voiceless is exactly what makes a god a god, which is the Kural’s comparison.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Striking match on ‘understanding the mute’ as divine; the page could not be fetched live, so it is paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aquinas argues that the secret thoughts of the heart, as they are in themselves, are known to God alone; angels and men can only conjecture them from bodily signs such as changes of face.
philosophy.explanation: He separates certain knowledge of hearts, which belongs to God, from inference by signs, which is open to creatures.
philosophy.tie_back: Aquinas sharpens the Kural’s point: to read signs without doubt is to come as close as a creature can to what belongs to God.
philosophy.source: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 57, a. 4
philosophy._accuracy_note: Excellent conceptual fit; Aquinas would deny a human full certainty, which Valluvar’s ‘without doubt’ claims.

kurals.tamil:
குறிப்பிற் குறிப்புணர் வாரை உறுப்பினுள்
யாது கொடுத்தும் கொளல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kurippir kurippunar vaarai uruppinul
Yaadhu koduththum kolal.
kurals.meaning: Those who can read inner intentions from outward signs should be secured as helpers, whatever part of one’s possessions must be given to win them.
kurals.elementary: If a football team finds a player who always knows where a teammate will pass before the ball is kicked, the coach will do almost anything to keep that player. Valluvar says a leader should treat people who read signals the same way.
kurals.university: The phrase kurippir kurippu unarvaar is the chapter’s technical formula, repeated in 705: ‘those who perceive the kurippu by means of kurippu’. Parimelazhagar takes the first kurippu as the outward signs (of face and eye) and the second as the inner intention they betray; Pope and Drew follow a further gloss in which the reader uses the indications of his own mind as a key to another’s. Uruppu here means the constituent ‘limbs’ of a kingdom (arasu uruppu: army, people, treasury, ministers, allies, forts, as set out in ch. 39), so yaadhu koduththum kolal is ‘secure them by giving whichever of these is asked’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read it as ‘giving anything among the country’s possessions’. The advice sits in a long Indian tradition of the king paying any price for an able minister. Uruppu will recur in 704 and 705 in the bodily sense (limbs, sense-organs), a deliberate word-play.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On first meeting Hanuman, Rama tells Lakshmana that Hanuman’s speech shows deep learning and discernment, and that a king with such a messenger will have every undertaking succeed.
hinduism.explanation: Rama recognises at once that Hanuman reads situations and people with rare skill and values him accordingly.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Ramayana treats such a perceptive helper as worth securing at any cost.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Fits the ‘prize such a helper’ theme; Rama praises eloquence and learning more than sign-reading as such.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out.”
christianity.explanation: A person’s real purpose lies deep and hidden, and only a discerning person can bring it to the surface.
christianity.tie_back: The ‘man of understanding’ who draws out hidden purposes is the helper the Kural says to acquire at any price.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the skill but says nothing about what a ruler should pay for it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the king said, ‘Bring him to me; I will appoint him exclusively for myself.’ And when he spoke to him, he said, ‘Indeed, you are today established [in position] and trusted.’”
islam.explanation: After Joseph reads the meaning hidden in the king’s dream, the king takes him out of prison and appoints him to his personal service.
islam.tie_back: The king does what the Kural advises: when he finds a man who reads hidden meanings, he secures him at once and at great cost.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on the ruler acquiring a discerner; Joseph reads a dream, not a face.

judaism.quote_or_event: The queen tells Belshazzar about Daniel, a man of excellent spirit who explains riddles and dissolves doubts; the king summons him, offers purple, a gold chain and third rank in the kingdom, and gives them to him.
judaism.explanation: A king faced with an unreadable sign pays the highest price to bring in the one man who can read it.
judaism.tie_back: Belshazzar’s rewards illustrate ‘give whatever it takes’ for a reader of signs.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the price paid; the sign is writing on a wall, not a human face.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Maha-Ummagga Jataka, King Vedeha hears of the boy Mahosadha’s uncanny discernment, brings him to court despite his rivals, and makes him his chief adviser.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta as Mahosadha repeatedly reads the hidden intentions of rivals and enemy kings and saves the kingdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The story is the Kural’s advice in narrative form: a king who wins such a discerner at any cost is saved by him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close fit in statecraft; the Jataka stresses cleverness in general rather than face-reading.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon praises Nestor’s counsel and wishes he had ten such counsellors among the Achaeans, saying Troy would then soon fall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The commander values one wise adviser above many warriors.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon’s wish is the Greek version of ‘acquire such men whatever it costs’.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Values a counsellor highly, but Nestor’s gift is advice and experience rather than reading unspoken signs.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli says the first judgement of a ruler’s intelligence is the quality of those around him, and distinguishes minds that understand for themselves, minds that grasp what others understand, and useless minds.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, choosing perceptive ministers is itself the proof of a prince’s wisdom.
philosophy.tie_back: Both Machiavelli and Valluvar make securing perceptive servants a top royal priority.
philosophy.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 22 (trans. W. K. Marriott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; about ministerial intelligence generally rather than sign-reading specifically.

kurals.tamil:
குறித்தது கூறாமைக் கொள்வாரோ டேனை
உறுப்போ ரனையரால் வேறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kuriththadhu kooraamaik kolvaarodu enai
Uruppor anaiyaraal veru.
kurals.meaning: Those who grasp what another intends without being told, and those who cannot, may look alike in body, yet they are different kinds of people.
kurals.elementary: Two phones can look exactly the same on the outside, but one has a smart app that understands your voice and the other does not. People are like that too: two people can look alike, but one understands what you mean without words and the other does not.
kurals.university: Kuriththadhu is ‘what (someone) has in mind’, and kooraamaik kolvaar ‘those who take it in without its being spoken’. Enai = the others (ஏனை), and uruppu or anaiyar (உறுப்பு ஓர் அனையர்) means ‘alike in limbs’, i.e., in bodily form; aal (ஆல்) is concessive (‘though’), and veru ‘they are different’. Parimelazhagar supplies the implied contrast: they are different in understanding (arivu), so the bodily likeness is misleading. The couplet quietly shifts uruppu from 703’s political ‘limbs of the kingdom’ to the body’s limbs. Commentators link it with the Kural’s repeated claim that the unperceptive are human only in form (compare 993 and the chapter on folly), and with the Sanskrit maxim that intelligence shows itself in grasping what is unsaid. The sandhi text reads ‘யுறுப்போ ரனையரால்’; there are no variants of meaning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that understandeth quickly, listeneth patiently, pursueth his objects with judgment and not from desire and spendeth not his breath on the affairs of others without being asked, is said to possess the foremost mark of wisdom”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura tells King Dhritarashtra that quick understanding is the first sign that separates the wise (pandita) from the rest.
hinduism.tie_back: Vidura, like Valluvar, uses quickness of understanding to divide people who otherwise look the same.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in spirit; Vidura speaks of quick understanding in general, not of reading unspoken intent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.”
christianity.explanation: The letter contrasts spiritual infants with mature people whose perception has been trained by practice.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it divides people not by appearance but by trained powers of discernment.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of a hidden difference in discernment, but is about moral maturity, not reading people.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if We willed, We could show them to you, and you would know them by their mark; but you will surely know them by the tone of [their] speech.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is told he will recognise the hypocrites, who look like everyone else, from subtle signs in how they speak.
islam.tie_back: People who look identical are told apart by the perceptive, which is exactly the Kural’s contrast.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on perceiving through outward signs; the verse is about exposing hypocrites, not about ranking the perceivers.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah lists seven traits that mark a golem (an uncultivated person) and seven that mark a wise person, such as not interrupting, answering to the point, and knowing what one has not understood.
judaism.explanation: Wisdom is defined by how a person listens and takes in what others say, not by status or appearance.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say that the real difference between people lies in how they understand others, not in how they look.
judaism._accuracy_note: Parallel contrast of wise and boorish; does not mention grasping the unspoken.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches that a person’s virtue, purity, endurance and discernment can be known only through long association, and only by one who is attentive and discerning, not by one who is not.
buddhism.explanation: The ability to see what others are really like belongs to the discerning person and not to others.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta, like the Kural, draws a line between those who perceive what lies beneath and those who cannot.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on the perceiver’s rarity; stresses long observation rather than instant reading.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “so true is it that the gods do not grace all men alike in speech, person, and understanding.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus rebukes the handsome but tactless Euryalus, saying one man may look plain yet be gifted in mind, while another looks like a god but lacks sense.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus makes the Kural’s point: outward form is no guide to the powers of the mind.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close on ‘alike in body, different in understanding’; not specifically about reading intentions.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle separates understanding (synesis) and considerate judgement (gnome), the capacity to grasp and fairly judge what others say and mean, from other intellectual virtues, noting that people are praised as ‘understanding’ for it.
philosophy.explanation: He treats the grasp of another’s meaning as a distinct excellence that some people have and others lack.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle, like Valluvar, names the faculty that makes people who look alike very different.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.10-11 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Conceptual parallel only; Aristotle discusses judging what is said, not what is left unsaid.

kurals.tamil:
குறிப்பிற் குறிப்புணரா வாயின் உறுப்பினுள்
என்ன பயத்தவோ கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kurippir kurippunaraa vaayin uruppinul
Enna payaththavo kan.
kurals.meaning: If the eyes cannot read a person’s intention from outward signs, what use are they, among all the body’s organs?
kurals.elementary: What good is a flashlight if you never switch it on? Your eyes are for more than seeing colours and shapes. They are meant to notice when someone is sad, worried or happy. If they never notice that, it is as if the flashlight stays off.
kurals.university: The couplet repeats 703’s formula kurippir kurippu unar- in the negative (unaraa vaayin, ‘if they do not perceive’) and turns it on the eye itself. Uruppinul (‘among the organs’) now plainly means the body’s members, and enna payaththavo is a rhetorical ‘of what profit are they?’ Parimelazhagar explains that the eyes are the foremost of the sense-organs, and their special excellence is to catch another’s mind through the signs of face and eye; if they cannot do that they are no better than the other limbs. Drew and Pope render ‘if they cannot by their own indications dive those of another’, reflecting the reading that the eye both shows and reads kurippu. The rhetorical question anticipates 710, where the eye becomes the only measuring rod. The sandhi text reads குறிப்புணரா வாயி னுறுப்பினு / ளென்ன பயத்தவோ கண்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that he cannot see Krishna’s true form with his own eyes and grants him a divine eye to see it.
hinduism.explanation: Ordinary sight is shown to be inadequate for seeing what really matters until it is given a deeper power.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say that eyes which only see surfaces fall short of their true purpose.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Loose parallel: about seeing the divine, not reading people.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Why reason ye, because ye have no bread? perceive ye not yet, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened? Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his disciples about the ‘leaven’ of the Pharisees, and they take it literally; he rebukes them for missing his meaning.
christianity.tie_back: Jesus asks the Kural’s own question: what are eyes for if they miss the meaning behind the sign?
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: listeners who miss an unspoken meaning are called eyed but unseeing.

islam.quote_or_event: “For indeed, it is not eyes that are blinded, but blinded are the hearts which are within the breasts.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the real failure of sight lies in the heart’s inability to understand what the eyes see.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, eyes that take in signs without understanding them are no better than blind.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on useless sight; the signs meant are God’s signs in history rather than human expressions.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding, that have eyes, and see not, that have ears, and hear not”
judaism.explanation: The prophet rebukes a people who have every faculty of perception yet grasp nothing of what is happening.
judaism.tie_back: Jeremiah and Valluvar both mock eyes that see without understanding.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same image of useless eyes; the context is spiritual obtuseness, not social perception.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Shortly before his passing, the Buddha gives Ananda a broad hint that he could remain for an aeon if asked, but Ananda, his mind distracted, fails to grasp the sign and does not ask.
buddhism.explanation: Even the Buddha’s closest attendant misses a plain signal, and the chance is lost.
buddhism.tie_back: The episode shows the Kural’s point: failing to read an intended signal makes one’s eyes and ears useless at the moment they matter most.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Excellent match on a missed hint; the canon blames Mara’s influence rather than simple dullness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Oedipus taunts the blind prophet Tiresias as blind in ears, mind and eyes, while Tiresias answers that Oedipus has sight yet cannot see the evil he is in.
greek_mythology.explanation: The man with working eyes misses every sign, while the blind seer understands everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Sophocles dramatises the Kural’s question: eyes that cannot read the signs are worthless.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; the signs are fate and oracles rather than a person’s face.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus says that eyes and ears are poor witnesses for people whose souls do not understand their language.
philosophy.explanation: The senses deliver signs, but only an understanding mind can read them.
philosophy.tie_back: Heraclitus states the principle behind the Kural: sight without understanding gives no knowledge.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in principle; paraphrased rather than quoted because the wording was not checked live.

kurals.tamil:
அடுத்தது காட்டும் பளிங்குபோல் நெஞ்சம்
கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aduththadhu kaattum palingupol nenjam
Kaduththadhu kaattum mukam.
kurals.meaning: Just as clear crystal takes on the colour of whatever is placed next to it, the face shows whatever is strongest in the heart.
kurals.elementary: Put a clear glass marble next to a red flower and the marble looks red. Put it next to a leaf and it looks green. Your face is like that marble. Whatever feeling is strongest inside you shows through it.
kurals.university: Palingu (Sanskrit sphatika) is clear rock-crystal, and aduththadhu kaattum means ‘shows what is next to it’: the crystal has no colour of its own but displays the hue of its neighbour. This is the famous Indian sphatika image (the crystal beside a red japa flower) used in Sankhya and Vedanta for how the pure self seems coloured by what it is near; Valluvar turns it into a psychology of expression. Kaduththadhu is glossed by Parimelazhagar as mikkadhu, ‘what is uppermost or abounding’ (from kadu-, to be intense), so the face shows the dominant feeling, not every passing thought. Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘what abounds in the heart’, and Pope renders ‘what’s throbbing in the mind’. The couplet grounds the chapter’s claim that kurippu can be read: the face is an honest medium. Sandhi text: பளிங்குபோ னெஞ்சங் / கடுத்தது காட்டும் முகம்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The internal (working of the) mind is perceived through the aspect, the motions, the gait, the gestures, the speech, and the changes in the eye and of the face.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the king presiding over a court how to read witnesses and litigants from their outward signs.
hinduism.tie_back: Manu, like Valluvar, treats the face and eyes as reliable displays of the inner mind.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-direct doctrinal match, in the same royal context.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The heart of a man changeth his countenance, whether it be for good or evil: and a merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance.”
christianity.explanation: Ben Sira observes that the face changes according to the state of the heart, for good or for ill.
christianity.tie_back: Sirach states the Kural’s rule almost word for word: the heart shows on the face.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; Sirach is in the Catholic and Orthodox Christian canon and is Apocrypha for Protestants.

islam.quote_or_event: “Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration.”
islam.explanation: The inner devotion of the Prophet’s companions is described as visibly marked on their faces.
islam.tie_back: What fills the heart shows on the face, as the Kural’s crystal shows its neighbour’s colour.
islam._accuracy_note: Face shows the inner state, but the mark here is devotion built up over time rather than a passing feeling.

judaism.quote_or_event: “As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs uses the image of a reflection in water to show how one heart mirrors or reveals another.
judaism.tie_back: Both use a reflecting medium to explain how the heart becomes visible.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong shared mirror image; Proverbs is about hearts reflecting each other more than faces showing hearts.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha illustrates knowledge of others’ minds with the image of a young person checking their face in a clean mirror or a bowl of clear water and seeing at once whether there is a blemish.
buddhism.explanation: A trained mind sees another’s state, passionate or free, as plainly as a face in a mirror.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural and the sutta both use a clear reflecting surface to show how visible an inner state is.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking shared mirror image; in the sutta the mirror stands for the knower’s clarity, not for the other person’s face.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He sat himself down away from the ships with a face as dark as night, and his silver bow rang death as he shot his arrow in the midst of them.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollo’s anger at the insult to his priest is visible on his face before it is released in the plague.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Even the god’s face shows the rage that fills him, as the Kural says every face shows its heart.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates face revealing feeling, but no one is shown reading it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero tells orators that the whole effect of delivery depends on the face, since the face is the image of the mind and the eyes its interpreters.
philosophy.explanation: Rhetoric depends on the fact that the face displays the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s ‘image of the mind’ is the Kural’s crystal in Roman form.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close idea; the Latin (imago animi vultus, indices oculi) is well attested, but the English is paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
முகத்தின் முதுக்குறைந்தது உண்டோ உவப்பினும்
காயினும் தான்முந் துறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mukaththin mudhukkuraindhadhu undo uvappinum
Kaayinum thaanmun thurum.
kurals.meaning: Is anything more knowing than the face? Whether a person is pleased or angry, the face announces it first.
kurals.elementary: When you get a present you love, your smile arrives before you can say ‘thank you’. When you are cross, your frown shows up before any words. Your face is like a messenger who always runs ahead of you.
kurals.university: Mudhukkuraindhadhu comes from mudhukkurai(mai), a Tamil idiom for mature wisdom or sagacity (literally ‘old-shortened’, an idiom whose sense is ‘wise beyond years’); the question ‘is there anything wiser than the face?’ credits the face with a kind of intelligence. Uvappinum kaayinum (‘whether it rejoices or burns with anger’) names the two poles of emotion, and thaan mun urum means ‘it comes forward first’, before speech or deliberate action. Parimelazhagar comments that the face runs ahead of the mind in disclosing liking and dislike, which is why it is called wise: it seems to know first. The irony is deliberate: the face is ‘wise’ precisely because it cannot keep a secret. Sandhi text: முதுக்குறைந்த துண்டோ வுவப்பினுங் / காயினுந் தான்முந் துறும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: On seeing his kinsmen drawn up for battle, Arjuna says his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles and his hair stands on end.
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna’s inner turmoil shows in his body before he has made any decision.
hinduism.tie_back: As the Kural says, the body and face announce the mind’s state before words or decisions.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good on the body betraying emotion first; the Gita describes the whole body, not only the face.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell. And the LORD said unto Cain, Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen?”
christianity.explanation: Cain’s anger and resentment show on his face before he acts.
christianity.tie_back: Cain’s fallen face runs ahead of his deed, exactly as the Kural says the face runs ahead of the mind.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match: anger visible on the face before speech or action.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Aisha he can tell her mood from a small change in how she swears: ‘by the Lord of Muhammad’ when pleased, ‘by the Lord of Abraham’ when angry.
islam.tie_back: Pleasure and anger leak out ahead of any declaration, and a loving observer reads them.
islam._accuracy_note: Captures the pleased-or-angry pair exactly, but the sign is a turn of speech, not the face.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Ilai teaches that a person’s character is recognised by three things: his cup, his pocket and his anger (koso, kiso, ka‘aso).
judaism.explanation: How someone behaves when drinking, when paying and when angry reveals what they really are.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Talmud treats moments of strong feeling such as anger as the times when the inner person shows through.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that anger reveals character, but says nothing specific about the face.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha, seeing Sariputta approach, remarks that his faculties are clear and his complexion pure and bright, and asks what meditation he has been practising.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha reads Sariputta’s inner state from his face before Sariputta says a word.
buddhism.tie_back: Sariputta’s face announces his inner calm first, and the Buddha reads it, as the Kural describes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fit on the face showing the mind; the state shown is serene joy rather than pleasure or anger.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “His heart was black with rage, and his eyes flashed fire as he scowled on Calchas”
greek_mythology.explanation: When the seer blames him for the plague, Agamemnon’s fury is visible in his eyes and scowl before he speaks.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Agamemnon’s face runs ahead of his words, as the Kural says it always does in anger.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close: anger shows in the face before speech.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Wittgenstein remarks that the human body is the best picture of the human soul, and elsewhere that we see emotion in a face directly rather than inferring it from facial contortions.
philosophy.explanation: For Wittgenstein, expression is not a clue from which we reason; the feeling is visible in the face itself.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s ‘wise face’: the face presents the feeling immediately, ahead of any report.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong philosophical parallel; paraphrased from well-known remarks, not checked live.

kurals.tamil:
முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும் அகம்நோக்கி
உற்ற துணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mukamnokki nirka amaiyum akamnokki
Utradhu unarvaarp perin.
kurals.meaning: If you have people who look into your heart and grasp what has happened to you, it is enough simply to stand before them and let them see your face.
kurals.elementary: When you come home after a bad day, a good parent can often tell just by looking at you. You don’t have to explain; you just stand there, and they already know you need a hug. Valluvar says that is what great helpers are like.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two ‘lookings’: mukam nokki (looking at the face) and akam nokki (looking into the heart). Nirka amaiyum means ‘it suffices to stand’, and utradhu is ‘what has befallen’ (a trouble or need). Parimelazhagar makes the king the one who stands: if he has ministers able to look into his mind and perceive what has occurred, he need not voice his trouble; standing and looking at their faces is enough, and they will understand and remedy it. Some modern readers (e.g., Kalaignar) generalise it to anyone who can read hearts. The couplet is the practical payoff of 701 and 703: the value of the perceptive minister is that the ruler is spared the need to speak, which in court may itself be dangerous. Variant spelling: ytamizh prints முகம்நோக்கி, the sandhi edition முகநோக்கி நிற்க வமையு மகநோக்கி.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The poor Brahmin Sudama visits his boyhood friend Krishna but is too ashamed to ask for help; Krishna understands his need unspoken and sends him home to find his hut turned into a mansion.
hinduism.explanation: Sudama asks for nothing; his presence is enough for Krishna, who reads his heart.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s scene exactly: standing before one who reads hearts is enough.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative match; the reader of hearts is God rather than a minister.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers not to pile up words in prayer, since God already knows their needs.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, one who knows the heart makes spoken requests unnecessary.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same logic of needs known without asking; the knower is God, not a human helper.

islam.quote_or_event: “Finally Abu-l-Qasim (the Prophet) passed by me and he smiled when he saw me, for he knew what was in my heart and on my face.”
islam.explanation: Abu Hurayrah, starving, hints at his hunger to others who miss it; the Prophet reads it on his face and feeds him.
islam.tie_back: Abu Hurayrah only had to stand before the right person; his face was enough, as the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: need read from the face, unspoken, by the perceptive one while others missed it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it was so, when the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, that she obtained favour in his sight ... Then said the king unto her: ‘What wilt thou, queen Esther? for whatever thy request, even to the half of the kingdom, it shall be given thee.’”
judaism.explanation: Esther risks her life simply by standing uninvited before the king; seeing her, he understands she has an urgent request before she speaks.
judaism.tie_back: Esther only has to stand before the king’s gaze, and her unspoken purpose is recognised.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit on standing silently before one who perceives; the king senses a request but not its content.

buddhism.quote_or_event: After his awakening the Buddha inclines not to teach; Brahma Sahampati, knowing the Buddha’s thought with his own mind, appears before him and begs him to teach.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says nothing aloud; the deity perceives his unspoken inclination and responds.
buddhism.tie_back: An unspoken inner state is perceived and answered by one who looks into the mind, as the Kural describes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Mind-reading leads to help, but the roles differ: the reader is a god appealing to the Buddha.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “You know it; why tell you what you know well already?”
greek_mythology.explanation: When Thetis rises from the sea to her weeping son, Achilles says she already knows his grief without being told.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles only has to be seen by one who knows his heart; explanation is unnecessary.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Captures ‘no need to speak’, though Thetis first asks and Achilles then explains at length.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Adam Smith argues that we come to feel what another feels by imaginatively placing ourselves in their situation, so that a sympathetic observer grasps a sufferer’s state from their circumstances and looks.
philosophy.explanation: Sympathy is the faculty that lets one person understand another’s condition without full explanation.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s perceptive helper is Smith’s sympathetic spectator at work.
philosophy.source: Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments I.i.1
philosophy._accuracy_note: Gives the mechanism rather than the ruler-minister setting.

kurals.tamil:
பகைமையும் கேண்மையும் கண்ணுரைக்கும் கண்ணின்
வகைமை உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pakaimaiyum kenmaiyum kannuraikkum kannin
Vakaimai unarvaarp perin.
kurals.meaning: To those who understand the different kinds of glances, the eyes themselves will tell whether a person is an enemy or a friend.
kurals.elementary: A dog can tell if you are friendly by the way you look at it. Soft eyes mean ‘friend’, a hard stare means ‘watch out’. Wise people learn to read eyes the same way, and the eyes tell them who is a friend and who is not.
kurals.university: Pakaimai (enmity) and kenmai (friendship, intimacy) are the two things kan uraikkum, ‘the eye will declare’. The condition is kannin vakaimai unarvaar, ‘those who perceive the varieties (vakai) of the eye’, i.e., the different kinds of look. Parimelazhagar applies it to foreign policy: if the king has ministers who can read the movements of the eye, the eyes of other kings and their envoys will themselves reveal hostility or friendship. Drew’s translation, following him, adds ‘(of foreign kings)’. Commentators link the verse with the Kural’s treatment of hidden enmity (ch. 89, Utpakai) and false friendship (ch. 83), where a smiling face may cover hostility: the eye is harder to disguise than the mouth. Sandhi text: பகைமையுங் கேண்மையுங் கண்ணுரைக்குங் கண்ணின் / வகைமை யுணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Angry appearance when the courtier is in sight; evading or refusal to hear his speech; no inclination to give him a seat or to see him; change in syllables and accents while talking to him; seeing with one eye; brow-beating ...”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya lists the signs by which a courtier can tell that the king has turned against him, many of them in the eyes and brows.
hinduism.tie_back: Kautilya catalogues the ‘varieties of the eye’ that, as the Kural says, reveal enmity to the trained observer.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close: a practical manual of reading hostility and favour from looks, in the same court setting.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.”
christianity.explanation: After Peter’s third denial, a single look from Jesus tells Peter everything, and he goes out and weeps.
christianity.tie_back: A look carries a whole message of relationship without words, as the Kural says eyes speak friendship and estrangement.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shows a glance speaking volumes; the look conveys love and reproach rather than enmity or alliance.

islam.quote_or_event: “Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater. We have certainly made clear to you the signs, if you will use reason.”
islam.explanation: Believers are warned that hostile outsiders give away their enmity through outward signs, if one pays attention.
islam.tie_back: Enmity shows through outward signs to the attentive, which is the Kural’s claim about the eye.
islam._accuracy_note: Good on hidden hostility betraying itself; the sign here is speech rather than the eye.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Jacob beheld the countenance of Laban, and, behold, it was not toward him as beforetime.”
judaism.explanation: Jacob reads in his father-in-law’s face that friendship has turned to hostility, and decides to leave.
judaism.tie_back: Jacob does exactly what the Kural describes: he reads enmity in a face and acts on it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on reading a changed friendship in the face.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha teaches Sigala how to tell false friends, such as the flatterer and the one who only talks, from true friends, by the signs in their behaviour.
buddhism.explanation: Friendship and enmity in disguise can be recognised by those who know what to look for.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta teaches that friend and foe can be told apart from their signs.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel aim; the signs are conduct over time, not glances.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “whereon Minerva went up to Ulysses and prompted him to beg pieces of bread from each one of the suitors, that he might see what kind of people they were, and tell the good from the bad”
greek_mythology.explanation: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus goes round the suitors to learn from their looks and conduct which are friendly and which hostile.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus is the Kural’s trained observer, sorting friend from foe by watching them.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on discerning friend from foe by observation; the signs are actions as well as looks.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is a point of cunning, to wait upon him with whom you speak, with your eye; as the Jesuits give it in precept: for there be many wise men, that have secret hearts, and transparent countenances.”
philosophy.explanation: Bacon advises watching the eyes and face of the person you negotiate with, because even guarded people give themselves away there.
philosophy.tie_back: Bacon’s ‘secret hearts, transparent countenances’ is the Kural’s point that the eye tells what the tongue hides.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close; Bacon files it under cunning rather than wisdom, a more cynical framing.

kurals.tamil:
நுண்ணியம் என்பார் அளக்குங்கோல் காணுங்கால்
கண்ணல்லது இல்லை பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Nunniyam enpaar alakkungol kaanungaal
Kannalladhu illai pira.
kurals.meaning: Look closely at those who call themselves perceptive, and you will find that the only measuring rod they use on others is the eye; there is nothing else.
kurals.elementary: A builder uses a ruler to measure wood. A person who is good at understanding others uses a different ruler: their eyes. By watching carefully, they measure what someone is feeling.
kurals.university: Nunniyam enpaar are ‘those who say, we are subtle (nunmai)’, i.e., who claim fine discernment. Alakkungol is ‘the rod with which they measure’ (alakkum kol), and kaanungaal ‘when one examines it’. Parimelazhagar, as usual, applies it to ministers: the measuring rod of those who claim to know others’ minds turns out, on inspection, to be nothing but their eyes. There is a double sense that commentators note: the minister measures by his own eye, and what he measures is the other person’s eye (continuing 709). The closing kan alladhu illai pira (‘there is nothing other than the eye’) sums up the chapter, which moves from praise of the perceptive (701-704) to the face (706-707) and finally the eye (705, 709-710) as the decisive sign. Sandhi text: நுண்ணிய மென்பா ரளக்குங்கோல் காணுங்காற் / கண்ணல்ல தில்லை பிற.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known verse of the Panchatantra (also in the Hitopadesha) says that even an animal understands what is spoken, but the wise infer what is unspoken, for the fruit of intelligence is knowing the gestures of others (parengita-jnana-phala hi buddhayah).
hinduism.explanation: Classical Sanskrit niti literature defines intelligence itself as the ability to read others’ unspoken signs.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make reading signs the real measure of a subtle mind.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong doctrinal match; paraphrased from the Sanskrit verse rather than a checked translation, and it stresses gestures in general, not only the eye.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus calls the eye the lamp of the body, the organ through which the whole person is lit or darkened.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts give the eye a unique, measuring role over the whole person.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the primacy of the eye, but Jesus speaks of moral vision, not of reading other people.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.”
islam.explanation: The word translated ‘those who discern’ (al-mutawassimin) means those who read marks, and classical exegetes connected it to firasa, the believer’s insight into people.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an honours those who read signs, the same people the Kural says measure by the eye.
islam._accuracy_note: The link to firasa is exegetical; the verse itself concerns lessons from a destroyed people.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah says that the disciples of Abraham have a good eye, while the disciples of Balaam have an evil eye, making the eye the index of a person’s character.
judaism.explanation: In rabbinic idiom the eye (ayin tovah, ayin ra‘ah) reveals whether a person is generous or grudging.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the rabbis treat the eye as the clearest measure of what lies inside.
judaism._accuracy_note: Idiomatic rather than literal: ‘good eye’ means generosity, not a readable glance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha speaks of three eyes: the eye of flesh, the divine eye, and the unsurpassed eye of discernment (pañña-cakkhu).
buddhism.explanation: Real seeing, for the Buddha, is the eye of wisdom that sees things as they are.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts make ‘the eye’, rightly trained, the true instrument of subtle knowledge.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Metaphorical eye of wisdom, not the literal eye reading faces.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Achilles turned in amaze, and by the fire that flashed from her eyes at once knew that she was Minerva.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles recognises the disguised goddess Athena at once by the look of her eyes alone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: For Achilles, as for Valluvar’s discerning minister, the eye is the one sure test.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good image of the eye as the decisive sign; it concerns identity rather than intention.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The ancient Physiognomonics attributed to Aristotle holds that character can be inferred from bodily signs, and that the region around the eyes, forehead, head and face is the most reliable place to look.
philosophy.explanation: Greek physiognomy made the eyes the chief evidence for reading a person.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a systematic version of the Kural’s claim that the eye is the discerner’s only measuring rod.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in its focus on the eyes; physiognomy reads fixed character, whereas Valluvar means changing intentions.
